The key to most RTS games is in mechanics. Usually economics are most important (never be waiting for money), but also watch for combat mechanics (know the range, armor, and DPS of every unit).

You might also consider a philosophical approach and read Sun Tzu's Art of War. In RTS and in life, understanding your position and that of your competition is important to success and Sun Tzu is a great place to start thinking in those terms.

Depends on the RTS. RTS games have some of the most varied gameplay styles of any genre.

I haven't played COH but I've played my fair share of SC2 and a bit of AoE2.

SC2 is an 'actions per minute' fest, basically the more stuff you can do in less time the better you'll get. In general however this applies to all RTS games. But SC2 in particular requires really high apm because buildings have abilities, units have abilities, and you constantly have to be making decisions about what to research or build next because the pace of the game is so quick. SC2 1v1 matches rarely break the 30 minute mark from what I've seen.

AoE2 is much slower paced than starcraft 2, but it still has a lot of stuff going on. Few units have abilities besides just attacking so you don't need to micromanage everything as much as in starcraft, but AOE has extreme hard counters (units that absolutely decimate other types of units) where starcraft doesn't rely so much on hard counter units to win.

I don't like playing RTS games against people too much. I generally play lots of co-op matches and 1v1 bot matches. I've beaten the first two starcraft 2 games on brutal however and I can regularly beat the hardest AI that doesn't cheat in starcraft 2, so I'm not terrible, I just like RTS's as a casual game.

My advice, use hotkeys, I bind my production buildings based on what they build, so barracks on 0, factories on 9, starports on 8, etc. That way I can produce units without having to look at my base. I always bind my main building so I can build worker units the same way, and use abilities from that building if they have them. Keybinding production buildings probably helped me more than anything else.

What other people have said already is good advice though. Understanding the basics of the RTS you want to be good at is important so playing the single player campaigns will naturally force you to deal with challenges. If you are winning 100% of the time you need to turn up the difficulty. You should always be challenging yourself if you want to improve.

Here are some basic common things that apply to many RTS games:

1) Scout early, Scout often. The key to winning at RTS is knowledge. You need to know where your opponent is moving, and when. You need to know where his base is, and what his fortifications are. You need to know what his army is comprised of.

2) Constantly expand. Most RTS games revolve around one or more currencies. Having more currency allows you to do more. If the game has resource nodes you want to be constantly expanding to acquire new ones all the time. Do not be the guy who depletes a single resource node before moving on.

3) Learn unit counters. Virtually all RTS games work via a "rock, paper, scissors" style rules when it comes to units. You need to know what units are strong against, and what units are weak against. The more encyclopedic your knowledge of this, the easier it will be to adapt your army to counter your opponent.

4) Do not play with a monolithic army. A big mistake newbies make is that they put all their units in the same group and move them around as one big army. Don't do this. It makes it easy for your opponent to manipulate you in to moving your armies in to ambush attacks or leaving yourself undefended at key strategic locations.

5) Use unit groups and hotkeys. Unit groups are a staple feature of all RTS games. It makes a lot of sense even inside one group you intend to move together to assign several groups for different unit types in order to quickly switch between them to have more granular control over unit movements. If a unit type has a special ability, know the hotkeys for that ability and learn when it's appropriate to use it.

6) Time is a resource. The faster you're able to move around, and the more you're able to control at the same time the bigger the advantage you'll have. Learn your optimal build order (there may be more than one depending on the game, and the faction inside the game) to get a base up and running. Usually these build orders are discovered quickly by pro players, and can be researched pretty easily on the web.

7) Save and watch replays if your game supports it. A great way to stop making the same mistakes is to really look at your decisions and why they didn't work. Are you overextending? Not expanding fast enough? Using the wrong units? Falling prey to ambush or diversionary tactics? A replay can expose the weak points in your game and help you to close the gaps.

8) Don't overcommit. When attacking a point it often makes more sense to do it in waves. Don't commit your entire army to a single engagement if you can help it - always have reserves in case something goes very wrong.

9) In games where there is free-form base building, use more than one of the same structures to build units more quickly. Build these structures closer to the front line as you push. What's faster than one barracks producing soldiers? Two barracks producing soldiers.

10) Practice. Practice. Practice. RTS games are among one of the hardest and potentially most frustrating genres of games. They are often difficult to master. Find the one you like and make it your religion, then learn all you can and play lots. Play people better than you are and watch what they do. If you constantly play people you can beat, or people you're on par with you don't push yourself to grow.

Hope that helps, good luck!

StarCraft is probably the best way to get good, since it has ranked competitive play, coop/teamgames, built in replays and a system for clans etc. Get used to the game by playimg offline first, then play ranked, look for an active clan that wants new players or at least someone who can teach you, look up tutorials on how to play better (Team Liquid).

Before playing multiplayer try beating the hard AI. Find a hotkey setup that is efficient and comfortable for you. Learn one basic strategy and try to execute it well. Always spend your resources (make units, supply, buildings and upgrades) and scout.
